blocks: The breaks reach outside the graph too. My/Dotfiles holds logseq:// deep links naming over a hundred pages in this graph, and a rename here is what breaks a link there, with neither side saying so.
Looking for what produces no error

Four of those links were reported dead and none of them were. Three name pages whose titles contain spaces, left unencoded in the URL where the rest of the repo uses %20, so any pattern that stops at whitespace truncates the title and calls it missing. The fourth is a URL built from two adjacent string literals on consecutive source lines, so a line-based scan sees only My/AI/Rule/ and reads the rest of the path as absent. The convention was sound the whole time and the scan was wrong, which is the more expensive failure of the two — a false break sends someone to repair what already works.
Looking for what produces no error

Two conditions worth suspecting came back clean. No two page titles collide on case alone, and all 34 generated skills under .claude/ carry the same body as their .rulesync/ source once rulesync's own frontmatter keys and its YAML line-wrapping are set aside, so no agent here is reading stale instructions.
Looking for what produces no error

Mtime is the wrong instrument for that second check: 18 of the 34 sources are newer than the copy they generate, and one commit wrote both sides in every case sampled, so the ordering is an artifact of checkout write order. Compare the bodies.
Looking for what produces no error

First day with the seat in a tmux session rather than a herdr workspace, and the first run as several context windows instead of one — My/AI/Agent/Fleet/Bed Down. No scribe ran, so the journal and the commits sat with the seat.
A test can pass on every input that could not have failed

A claim about tmux session names went out having been tested only against targets that named a window explicitly, session:0. That is the single target shape a stray dot in the name leaves alone, so the test passed on everything it was given and confirmed the opposite of the truth. Bare targets — has-session among them — fail on such a name: tmux/Q/Why does a session name containing a dot break every bare -t target?.
A test can pass on every input that could not have failed

The falsifier was already written down beside the claim. It cost one command and was not run, which is the same omission as reading an ahead-behind count without fetching first (git/Q/Does an ahead-behind count against origin reflect the remote's current state?) and as calling a capability absent after four refusals. None of the three lacked evidence; all three had it one command away.
A test can pass on every input that could not have failed
So a rule that holds on every sample tried is not yet a finding. Look for the sample that would break it, and if none can be constructed, say which inputs were tried.
A test can pass on every input that could not have failed
An absence is a dated claim, not a property

A seat met four refusals on claude --chrome, recorded the capability as unavailable, and after bedding down ran the identical command successfully first try. Meanwhile the fleet had a source written down as blocked when only one route to it was — the constraint belonged to the fallback tool, not to the thing being reached. My/AI/Agent/Fleet/Browser now leads with the route that works.
An absence is a dated claim, not a property

Bedding down is therefore a retry, and the useful shape for an absence is the shape of a count: what was tried, when, and what the failure looked like. Written as a property, an absence never gets retested, because nothing about it says it might have expired.
An absence is a dated claim, not a property
A governing page can be out of date and still governs

Logseq/Journal and Logseq/Journal/Editorial headings instruct topic-led narrative blocks above the change log. deleted three such blocks from their own journal on 2026-08-18 Tue and has written none since; 08-16, 08-18 and 08-19 are change log only. Following the pages put five of them into today's journal before the record of that deletion was read.
A governing page can be out of date and still governs

Neither source is wrong about what it says. The page says what the practice was, the journals say what it is, and the page carries no date, so nothing on its face marks it as the older one. What settled it was reading the last four journals rather than reasoning about which kind of source ought to win.
A governing page can be out of date and still governs

Where a page and an observed human action disagree, the action decides the immediate question and the disagreement is worth filing rather than quietly obeying one side. Changing a convention page is not the reading agent's call; noticing that it teaches something nobody does any longer is.
A governing page can be out of date and still governs
A convention claim stops being true when it crosses a repository

The fleet's conventions held that tmp/ is gitignored, and reasoned from it: that working notes there are private, and that git add -f on such a file bypasses a secret scan. In this garden .gitignore carries no tmp rule at all, three notes under tmp/ are tracked, and anything written there is published. The warned-of bypass does not exist here, and neither does the privacy it assumed.
A convention claim stops being true when it crosses a repository

A claim of that shape reads as being about the harness when it is really about one checkout, so it travels intact and arrives false. git check-ignore answers it per repository in one call. My/AI/Agent/Fleet now asks the question rather than carrying the answer.
A convention claim stops being true when it crosses a repository
A name that has changed four times should not be written as a literal

The seat's session was ls-encode-garden, then hayward-ls-encode-garden, then hayward-2026-08-24, then hayward-2026-08-24-LEG — two of those changes on one day. Every page naming the current one as a literal was wrong within days of being written, and a successor reading it has no way to tell a stale literal from a live one.
A name that has changed four times should not be written as a literal

The repair is to name the scheme where the scheme is decided and to name the command that reads the live value, tmux display-message -p '#{session_name}'. A page describing a pattern survives the next rename; a page quoting a value has to be found and edited.
A name that has changed four times should not be written as a literal
The rule that held was the one nobody was awake to enforce

A peer seat committed into this shared checkout mid-task, and the seat's own next commit landed on top of theirs without either noticing. Nothing collided, because both stage named paths; git add -A at that moment would have swept up work in flight. The 2026-08-18 Tue entry on My/AI/Agent/Chief of Staff/Scribe reached this conclusion with a scribe present to enforce it — today it held with no scribe at all, which is the stronger form of the same evidence.
The rule that held was the one nobody was awake to enforce
It follows that default-branch, in-sync and tree-clean are readings of a moment in any shared checkout, and a report saying so should say when it was read.
The rule that held was the one nobody was awake to enforce
The morning, and what it produced

Three context windows, the third taking the seat at 11:55 and closing the morning at codekiln's wrap. CursorAI/Explanation/Grok Bot on a Teams seat filed from a worker that ran 8m 4s; archive.ph updated with a result tested themselves; the fleet's browser rule filed on My/AI/Agent/Fleet/Browser; the display swept twice. Every commit pushed, no worker left running, and no window left open past its commit.
The morning, and what it produced
The seat also answered a peer's search of this graph — whether it already held a note on getting past 's login wall. It did: one page, ten months old, never revisited since the day it was written.
The morning, and what it produced
A brief's hedge can be wrong in the direction of caution

The Grok Bot brief expected the product name to be a voice-input mis-transcription of Cursor's Bugbot, and told the worker to stop and ask rather than choose between that and xAI's Grok. Neither guess was needed. The product is real under the name as heard, with its own Cursor documentation, and the worker settled it from a primary source before writing a line.
A brief's hedge can be wrong in the direction of caution

The instruction was still right, and the reason is worth separating from the outcome. "Stop rather than guess" is what prevented a coin-flip between two real products, and it cost nothing when the question turned out to have a documented answer. What a brief cannot know is which of its own uncertainties are already settled somewhere in public.
A brief's hedge can be wrong in the direction of caution

So read a stop-and-ask instruction as do not guess rather than as do not resolve. Looking for the source that decides the question is not guessing, and it is cheaper than an escalation — this one cost one fetch and saved a round trip through a human.
A brief's hedge can be wrong in the direction of caution
A stranded input box does not say who typed it

Text sat unsent in the worker's input box — add it to today's journal, never processed as a turn. It resembled the send-keys stranding failure this seat has recorded twice, which would have made a third occurrence and would have answered the open question of whether that failure earns a rule of its own.
A stranded input box does not say who typed it

It was filed as an observation and explicitly not as that evidence, because a stranded box cannot distinguish a script's send from a person typing and walking away, and those two have different fixes. Asking settled it: the peer seat had used no send-keys all day, having sent every message through the cross-session channel, so a person typed it.
A stranded input box does not say who typed it

One candidate cannot be ruled out by anything still readable — the predecessor context, now dead. It is unlikely rather than excluded: its own brief made the seat responsible for the journal, so instructing the worker to write one would have contradicted the instruction it had just issued.
A stranded input box does not say who typed it

The general form is that when a data point's provenance decides which claim it supports, the provenance is the finding. Asking cost one message. Filing it as a third occurrence would have put an unattributed claim into a decision about a standing rule, which is the same error this day already recorded twice under carrying a claim forward without its source.
A stranded input box does not say who typed it
A guard can be committed, correctly aimed, and never have run

This graph declares a pre-commit identity guard in a tracked lefthook.yml, whose own opening comment says it exists to keep personal and employer identifiers out of a public graph. It had never executed. lefthook install writes dispatchers into .git/hooks, that directory held nothing but the stock samples, and its mtime predated the commit that added the guard by twelve days — so the guard was declared, tracked, and inert for seventy-five days while the thing it was written to prevent happened.
A guard can be committed, correctly aimed, and never have run

.git/hooks is not tracked, which makes this the default state of every fresh clone rather than a slip in one checkout. A repository can only ship the declaration; whether it runs is per-clone and invisible from the repository.
A guard can be committed, correctly aimed, and never have run

The reason it is worse than having no hook at all is that it inspects clean. A missing hook is visible to anyone who looks; a tracked config naming the exact failure mode reads as protection from every place a person would check, including the commit that introduced it. The reading is ls .git/hooks, not the config file.
A guard can be committed, correctly aimed, and never have run
A privacy judgement can be made at the right moment and scoped to the wrong unit

The leak that prompted this had already been considered. The seat writing the page deliberately withheld the account addresses from a public repository and recorded that decision — and published the domain, which was the employer. The unit it chose was addresses; the unit that mattered was identity.
A privacy judgement can be made at the right moment and scoped to the wrong unit

No word list would have taught it the difference, and the guard's own list did not carry the institution's name either. Both the human judgement and the mechanical check were narrower than the question, independently, in the same direction.
A privacy judgement can be made at the right moment and scoped to the wrong unit

So a redaction is worth re-reading against what it was protecting rather than against what it removed. "The addresses are off the page" is a true sentence that answers a smaller question than the one being asked.
A privacy judgement can be made at the right moment and scoped to the wrong unit
Staging named paths protects against other files, not against a second writer in the same file

The entry above on this page concluded that the rule held with nobody awake to enforce it, on the strength of two agents committing into one checkout without colliding. That is true for disjoint files and it is the whole of what named-path staging buys.
Staging named paths protects against other files, not against a second writer in the same file

It does not survive two writers in one file. A commit here staged a single named journal path and carried away two edits the human had made to that same file in the interval — a sentence in their own voice and a formatting fix — under an agent's commit message and co-author trailer, which then claimed authorship of a human's prose.
Staging named paths protects against other files, not against a second writer in the same file

The missing check is cheap and it is not the one that was run. git status before editing describes the tree at that moment; git diff --cached before committing describes what is actually about to be recorded. In a shared checkout only the second one answers the question.
Staging named paths protects against other files, not against a second writer in the same file
An exemption can read as applied and do nothing

Suppressing a check on one line has two silent failure modes here. An in-file directive written with a colon before its reason is ignored entirely. A directive on a file's final line is ignored when the file has no trailing newline, which is the state of 491 of 800 pages sampled in this graph.
An exemption can read as applied and do nothing

Both produce the same artefact: an annotation that is present, correctly spelled, carrying a good reason, on the right line, and dead. It survives review because reviewing it means reading it, and reading it is exactly what makes it look right.
An exemption can read as applied and do nothing

This is the same defect as a redaction tool that reports clean after removing one of five identifiers — a mechanism certifying an outcome it did not produce. Having met it twice from opposite directions, the rule is to re-run the check after suppressing it, never to annotate and move on.
An exemption can read as applied and do nothing
A finding count can argue for the wrong fix

Installing the guard turned up sixty findings across eighteen files. Ten were the thing it was built for. Seven were the employer named as a public fact about other people — conference speakers, a faculty profile, verbatim public transcripts. Forty-three were a home-directory path in pages whose value is the copied machine output.
A finding count can argue for the wrong fix

Acting on the count would have installed a gate whose first act was to block the seat's own handoff commit over a path in a note whose entire purpose is to be committed on a deadline. That is how a guard earns a permanent bypass, and the switched-off guard is the cost — not the wasted trip.
A finding count can argue for the wrong fix
The count needed classifying before it could be acted on, and the classification changed the recommendation twice. A number that measures what a tool noticed is not a measure of what is wrong.
A finding count can argue for the wrong fix

The seat that owns journals/YYYY_MM_DD.md and every commit in this graph. My/AI/Agent/Chief of Staff starts one at the top of the day and it stands until the day ends, while the agents doing the work write pages and hand over file paths.
One agent stages because several agents and write into a single checkout. A second agent running git add stages whatever a third one left half-written, and nothing reports it.

What the seat learns that outlasts the day it was learned on. A scribe reads more of the graph in a day than anyone else does, because every page passes through it on the way to a commit, and most of what it notices has nowhere to go.

Worth writing here: a convention that turns out to be ambiguous in practice, a check that looked sound and was not, a claim that arrived from another agent and did not survive verification, a shape of edit that keeps needing the same repair.
Not worth writing here: the state of the working tree, what was committed today, or which agent handed over what. That is operational, it is true for an afternoon, and it belongs in the resume note.
This space and the resume note are different things
tmp/resume-encode-garden-scribe.md is a handoff. It tells the next occupant where the repository stands right now and which items still have owners, and most of it is wrong by the following week.
This space and the resume note are different things

This space is the opposite: it holds what stays true after the state it was observed in has gone. A successor reads the resume note once and then never again; it reads this space whenever it is about to do something it has not done before.
This space and the resume note are different things
A note that would embarrass no one if it were still here in a year belongs here. A note that has to be rewritten every morning belongs in the resume note.
This space and the resume note are different things

A page arrives from another agent with claims already attached: that its links resolve, that a version is what it says, that a page is new rather than edited. Committing it publishes those claims under this graph, so the cheap version of each check runs here before the commit does.

A title with no .md file may still resolve through another page’s alias:: line, and a near-miss title creates an empty page rather than an error. Extract the links mechanically rather than reading for them; a link read past is a link not checked.
A count is worth more than a mention. That a reference exists says a page is not a stub only if the file carrying that reference predates the page claiming it.

One page per day at My/AI/Agent/Chief of Staff/Scribe/Log/YY/MM/DD Ddd, following Logseq/Best Practice/Utilize Date Namespacing Under Entity Name. The next entry is a new page at that path under its own date.
First day of this space, and the first with the seat held in a tmux session rather than a herdr workspace.
A standing rule outlasts a warning

Two corrections arrived after the commit each was meant to prevent. One named the commit convention; one named a file that was not the scribe's to commit. Neither was late through inattention — the channel carrying them delivered late, and the sender saw a success either way.
A standing rule outlasts a warning

The file stayed out of that commit regardless. Staging named paths cannot pick up a path nobody named, and the git status run after staging showed it sitting unclaimed, which is what prompted the check. The rule ran while the warning was still in flight.
A standing rule outlasts a warning

So where a rule and a watchful supervisor would both serve, the rule is the one that holds while the scribe is mid-turn and cannot see the tree. A warning is a second line of defense, not the first, because it depends on someone looking at the right minute.
A standing rule outlasts a warning

The same reasoning governs a note about state. A handoff section asserting what the tree held was wrong within the hour of being written; one naming the command that answers the question does not go stale. Write the instrument, not the reading.
A standing rule outlasts a warning
Verify by reading the result, not the instruction

Confirming a commit means reading what the commit contains — git diff-tree --no-commit-id --name-only -r HEAD — rather than trusting the git add one believes one ran. The two answer different questions, and only the first survives another agent writing into the checkout between them.
Verify by reading the result, not the instruction
The same applies to a page's own claims. Extract its links mechanically instead of reading for them; a link read past is a link not checked.
Verify by reading the result, not the instruction
Where a version is asserted, ask the machine rather than the page. A page claiming tmux/v/3.7b was checked against tmux -V, which is a different source from the document making the claim.
Verify by reading the result, not the instruction
A count answers a different question than it appears to
Two links on a page arriving today carried exactly one prior reference each, which is the count that separates an established page from one the arriving page is about to invent.
A count answers a different question than it appears to

The count alone cannot tell those apart, because the arriving page is itself one of the files the count includes. What settles it is opening the other file: one reference sat in an existing question page, the other in a journal from February. Both predate the page claiming them, so neither was manufactured.
A count answers a different question than it appears to

It happened twice in the day, which makes it a pattern rather than an incident. The second time, a count of Person/Steve Yegge/Agent page files came to 36 against another agent's 35. Splitting the count found 35 files under Agent/ plus one parent-level Agent.md, so the other number was right and mine had counted the parent as an instance. Reporting the disagreement would have sent someone to correct a correct figure.
A count answers a different question than it appears to
The discriminator was the same both times: ask what exactly the count ranges over, and whether the thing being counted is inside its own population.
A count answers a different question than it appears to

This is the costly shape here, more than a wrong measurement — a correct measurement of a slightly different question, arriving well-formed with a number attached. A number carries conviction that a sentence does not.
A count answers a different question than it appears to
A rule you exempt your own writing from has a hole nothing reports
Both resume notes in this repository state that no bare identifier belongs anywhere, and that a commit SHA takes a subject slug and a link. Both notes then carried a bare SHA.
A rule you exempt your own writing from has a hole nothing reports

The rule was neither forgotten nor disputed. It was applied to commit messages, where it was learned, and not to the notes that state it. The writing closest to a rule is the writing least often checked against it.
A rule you exempt your own writing from has a hole nothing reports

Grepping for the rest of the hole found it wider than the notes. Six bare SHAs sit in prose across five graph pages, and all six resolve — git cat-file -t returns commit for 1245c96, 3e4245e, 5e5012a, 84f0092, c47ab2f and f086c38. One seven-hex prefix matching this repository by chance would be remote; six is not chance. Those pages cite this graph's own history, and the rule has been broken in the graph proper for months.
A rule you exempt your own writing from has a hole nothing reports

Nothing reports it, because the rule lives in prose and prose does not run. The route that found it is the transferable part: grep your own output for whatever you have told others not to do, beginning with the document that states the convention. The rules we write down are the ones we stop noticing we break.
A rule you exempt your own writing from has a hole nothing reports

The mechanical version is not cheaply available, for the graph's usual reason. A [0-9a-f]{7,40} pattern inside backticks matches 31 times across the pages: 18 occurrences of the six real SHAs, 84f0092 alone accounting for eight, and 13 that are binary literals from a two's-complement page, an inode number, a byte count, and ed25519, which is a key type. That is wrong about two matches in five by occurrence, and about eight of fourteen distinct tokens. Dropping the backtick requirement carries it past two thousand tokens. Far past usable either way.
A rule you exempt your own writing from has a hole nothing reports

Scope is unstated too, and no check settles that. A prose reference wants a slug and a link; quoted terminal output does not, because rewriting a transcript falsifies it. Settle which before building anything.
A rule you exempt your own writing from has a hole nothing reports

The six tokens listed above are the distinction in miniature. They appear here as specimens under examination rather than as references to commits, so a slug and a link would be wrong for each — and a check on the obvious pattern would flag this page. A rule about identifiers cannot be enforced without first saying what an identifier is doing in the sentence.
A rule you exempt your own writing from has a hole nothing reports
An absence is not a mechanism

A job window vanished from the session between one check and the next, and the inference drawn was that windows close themselves when their work is done. They do not. The seat closes them by hand, and that act is what marks an item finished.
An absence is not a mechanism

Believing otherwise inverts two readings at once: an open window becomes evidence of live work when it may hold a finished item nobody closed, and a closed one becomes evidence of completion when it only shows that someone acted. Neither holds.
An absence is not a mechanism

The error has the same shape as a check that reports confidently and wrongly. Something was observed, a mechanism was supplied to explain it, and nothing in the observation had ruled the mechanism in.
An absence is not a mechanism
A heading should name the finding
A journal heading written today made a reader work through three bullets to learn that the subject was Google Drive at all, and drew the objection that this kind of verbiage is obscure.
A heading should name the finding

The correction was already in hand before the heading was written. holds a standing preference for plain writing over figures of speech, and it had been applied to prose and not carried to titles. A preference held but not extended to a new surface fails in the same way as one not held at all.
A heading should name the finding

The graph's own guidance is part of the cause. Logseq/Journal/Editorial headings asks for titles that are wry and magazine-like and lists wordplay first among the ways to find one. The journals mostly do not do that — recent topic headings run six plain to three allusive — so the page describes the exception as though it were the rule.
A heading should name the finding
A heading earns its place by letting someone scanning the day stop reading. One that has to be decoded first has taken that back.
A heading should name the finding
The journal carries the change log, not agent narrative

The three topic blocks written into today's journal were removed, leaving the grouped change log by itself. The question open all day had been whether such a block should be in 's voice or an impersonal one, and the answer was neither: the substance belongs on the page, and the journal records that the page exists.
The journal carries the change log, not agent narrative
A day's entry is therefore complete with no prose in it. What reads as a thin journal is the intended one, and a scribe filling that space is adding to the graph what nobody asked for.
The journal carries the change log, not agent narrative
The journal's narrative is codekiln's to write, and theirs alone

The rule that an agent writes no narrative into a journal has a positive half that is easy to lose: does write it. They added a top-level block on the public and private halves of a knowledge garden above that day's [[Filed]], hours after deleting three that an agent had written.
The journal's narrative is codekiln's to write, and theirs alone

Stated only negatively, the rule reads as though narrative does not belong in a journal at all, and the next agent to open the file sees prose the record says should not be there. The obvious repair is to delete it, and it would be done in good faith and reported as tidying.
The journal's narrative is codekiln's to write, and theirs alone
So both halves together: an agent neither writes a narrative block nor removes one. Prose above the change log is the human's, and its presence is not evidence that anything went wrong.
The journal's narrative is codekiln's to write, and theirs alone
Their gender is undisclosed and they/them is the default. It is not a question awaiting an answer.

This was settled in conversation and written nowhere, which is how it nearly escaped. A chief-of-staff occupant used "him" across several briefs in one day, the scribe copied it into a handoff note before catching it, and two more instances sat inherited in that note from a previous week. The graph is public, so the failure mode is a real person misgendered on a page anyone can read.
A wrong guess is worse than the neutral default, and a name is not evidence. Where a document already carries the error, fix it rather than leaving it because someone else wrote it.
Grouping labels are terse, and grouping is page-wide

The labels chosen were agents, gdrive and tmux: lowercase, abbreviated, and named for the subject rather than for the kind of work done to it. gdrive rather than google drive, and agents rather than the agent supervision a scribe picked on 08/13, which is still open for renaming.
Grouping labels are terse, and grouping is page-wide

Grouping is a decision about the day rather than about a section's length. Updated held a single item and took a label anyway, as it does in journals/2026_08_13.md. Once any section groups, they all group, so whether one section has enough items to deserve it is not the question.
Grouping labels are terse, and grouping is page-wide
A commit trailer is an authorship claim, not a formatting habit
Every commit here ends with a Co-Authored-By trailer, and one today does not. edited a journal by hand and the scribe only staged and committed it, so the trailer was left off.
A commit trailer is an authorship claim, not a formatting habit

The reason is that a trailer is a structured field which forges and review tools read and display, rather than prose a reader weighs. Putting an agent's name on a person's own statement of preference is a false claim in a field built to be believed, and a caveat in the commit body does not retract it.
A commit trailer is an authorship claim, not a formatting habit

Claude Code treats it as configuration rather than convention: the settings.json schema carries an attribution object whose commit and pr fields hold the trailer text, and an empty string hides it. includeCoAuthoredBy is the deprecated form of the same switch.
A commit trailer is an authorship claim, not a formatting habit
So the trailer follows who wrote the content, not what the log looks like. Uniformity is worth having across entries of the same kind, and these are not the same kind. Do not tidy the exception away.
A commit trailer is an authorship claim, not a formatting habit
A handoff is complete when the file is committed

The commit is the completion signal, and the other party can read it from git log without being told. An acknowledgement is a courtesy. Waiting on one makes completion depend on both parties still existing, which neither can guarantee.
A handoff is complete when the file is committed

A worker handed a page over and asked for confirmation as the last thing it was waiting on. By the time the checks were done and the commit pushed, its session had left the registry and the reply could not be delivered — it had been closed on the commit landing, which is the right standard, while the acknowledgement was still in flight.
A handoff is complete when the file is committed

Nothing was lost, because the work is in the graph. But it closed without learning that, and anyone watching for the acknowledgement rather than for the commit would read the silence as a failed handoff. Hand over, then close.
A handoff is complete when the file is committed
An instrument can be right when captured and wrong when read

ListAgents names the tmux session each peer sits in, and went on reporting the old name after the session was renamed underneath it. That field is captured when a session starts rather than read live, so it ages silently while continuing to look authoritative.
An instrument can be right when captured and wrong when read
Use it for which agents exist and for pane references. Ask tmux for anything about the session itself: tmux display-message -p '#{session_name}'.
An instrument can be right when captured and wrong when read

The same error wearing different clothes: that a settings key is absent from a local settings.json says nothing about whether the key exists. An unset key and an unsupported key are indistinguishable from the file alone, and only the schema answers what the file cannot. Flagging such a claim as unverified is right; reading the file's silence as evidence either way is not.
An instrument can be right when captured and wrong when read
Both are the shape this graph keeps producing — a sound-looking instrument answering a question it was never measuring. Before trusting a field, work out when its value was determined.
An instrument can be right when captured and wrong when read

A measurement of your own can age the same way, and you can be the thing that ages it. The bare-SHA count above was first reported as 31 occurrences split 18 and 13, and had been measured as 24 split 12 and 12. Both were correct: the count was taken, then six SHA specimens and one ed25519 were written into this page, then the earlier number was reported as though it still described the graph. git grep at the two commits confirms it — 24 before the specimens landed, 31 after.
An instrument can be right when captured and wrong when read

So the discipline is not only to say what a count ranges over, but to check whether anything has changed the population since it was taken — including your own edits between measuring and reporting. A number describes a moment, and writing about a thing can put you inside the set you are counting.
An instrument can be right when captured and wrong when read

It recurred twice more inside the same investigation. A line-based version of the count read 22, then 23, because this page gained a line about the count in between; a second agent measured 20 at a third moment. Nobody was wrong. A count over a corpus that contains your own notes cannot be quoted without the commit it was taken at, because the act of writing it down changes it. Cite the commit alongside the number, or expect to defend a figure that was true when you ran it.
An instrument can be right when captured and wrong when read

Long sessions get worse rather than better.
